# ADDENDUM 6 — June 23-30, 2026 (Investor Materials)

## 57. INVESTOR MATERIALS PRODUCED — pitch deck (English + Chinese) + one-pager

Three investor-facing deliverables produced this session, all built around the new brand identity (§58). Files: `NeuRobots_Investor_Pitch_Deck.pptx` (14 slides, English), `NeuRobots_Investor_Pitch_Deck_CN.pptx` (14 slides, Simplified Chinese for Mainland China investors/partners), `NeuRobots_One_Pager.docx` (single-page leave-behind). Deck structure: title → problem → solution (old way vs. NeuRobots way) → how it works (4 pillars) → market strategy (Phase 1 + Phase 2) → traction timeline → competition (Standard Bots head-to-head) → why us → business model → team → use of funds (bar chart) → the ask → roadmap → closing. Editorial design philosophy (distinct layouts per slide; no recycled card grids; oversized hero typography on title/closing/ask; navy + amber as structural elements, not decoration). Dark/light slide alternation creates rhythm. **Chinese version requires native Mandarin business-speaker review before live investor use** — AI translation is a strong starting point, not a final draft.

## 58. NEUROBOTS MANUFACTURING — name + brand identity

**Naming decision after extended iteration** (Arcwell → Neuroforge → Neurobots/Neurobotix/Neura family → settled on **NeuRobots Manufacturing**). Stylization is load-bearing: always capital R (`NeuRobots`), with the R rendered in amber in display type. This produces a deliberate visual wordplay readable two ways: **NEU + ROBOTS** ("new robots") and **NEURO + BOTS** ("smart robots"). Wordmark format: `NEU` + `R`(amber) + `OBOTS`, all-caps with letter-spacing. **Pending availability checks before final lock-in:** USPTO TESS in Class 7 (machines) + Class 9 (software); domains (neurobots.com almost certainly taken; backups: neurobotsmfg.com, neurobots-mfg.com, neurobots.io, neurobots.ai); Google/LinkedIn for direct robotics competitors.

**Logo:** node-based stylized "N" inside a navy circle. Four dots connected by lines representing a neural network; top-right node + descending line rendered in amber, evoking a spark of intelligence (echoes the amber R in wordmark). Asset: `logo_mark.png`.

**Color palette — "Deep Steel":**

| Role | Hex | Use |
|------|-----|-----|
| Steel (primary navy) | `#1B2A41` | Dark backgrounds, headlines on light |
| Steel Deep | `#0F1B2D` | Deepest navy for hero slides |

**Typography:** Arial throughout (safe-list font, renders reliably across PowerPoint installs); sentence case for body and bullets; editorial weight for headlines (64-96pt hero, 26-32pt slide titles); all-caps letter-spaced eyebrow labels (10-12pt bold) above slide titles.

## 59. POSITIONING CLARIFICATION — robot maker + AI platform (distinct from prior integrator framing)

**Important reconciliation with prior strategy doc.** `document_pdf.pdf` (in project files) positions this venture as an "AI-native automation integrator targeting mid-market manufacturers" — explicitly NOT a robot manufacturer ("We are not a robot manufacturer. We are not a humanoid robot company..."). The investor materials produced this session reflect a **different, current positioning**: NeuRobots makes the robots AND the AI brains (head-to-head with Standard Bots on hardware + software), with integration/services as an additional revenue line. The pivot is intentional and confirmed by the user; the integrator framing in `document_pdf.pdf` is superseded. Tagline: "Robots that learn by watching." Category positioning: robot manufacturer + AI platform with integration services as upsell. Closing line: "Let's teach the machines." One-sentence pitch: NeuRobots makes industrial robots with AI built in — robots that learn by watching a video instead of being programmed by certified engineers.

**Financial framing also pivoted.** Prior strategy doc staged: friends/family $250K-$750K → pre-seed $1.5M-$4M (after Phase 1) → Series A $8M-$15M (after Phase 2). Current ask: **$1M for 10% at ~$9M pre-money / $10M post-money** (priced round or SAFE w/ $10M cap). The $1M sits within the lower end of the prior staged plan but the valuation framing is more assertive — anchored to hot AI/robotics market conditions and Standard Bots' $1B valuation as the reference point. Have a negotiating floor of $6-7M pre-money in mind before walking into the room.

## 60. STANDARD BOTS — competitive intel + funding history

Best-funded direct competitor, marketing as "AI-native," U.S.-based design/assembly.

| Round | Amount | Date | Notes |
|-------|--------|------|-------|
| Series B | $63M | ~2024 | General Catalyst; valuation undisclosed |
| Series C | $200M | June 2026 | RoboStrategy + General Catalyst; $1B valuation; funding to quadruple Glen Cove NY manufacturing |
| **Total** | **$263M+** | | |

Sources: The Robot Report, Bloomberg, Forbes (June 2026).

**NeuRobots differentiation:** (1) In a live demo Teddy attended, Standard Bots did NOT show AI-driven robot training/programming despite "AI-native" positioning — NeuRobots has working program-by-demonstration today. (2) Camera-taught part recognition (their demo did not show this). (3) Program-by-demonstration removes programming entirely for many tasks; Standard Bots has not demonstrated this. (4) U.S. manufacturing — Standard Bots has 5-year roadmap to fully U.S.-made (backed by $200M); NeuRobots makes same commitment from smaller capital base. **Honest caveat for in-room delivery:** the "no AI training shown" point is based on one demo — frame as observation, not categorical claim, until corroborated.

## 62. OPERATIONS — Boyceville WI shop + Jade Molds test bed + China sourcing

**Boyceville, WI shop** — in-house machining, fabrication, and assembly. Where Teddy leads hardware build-out of robot bases, end-of-arm tooling, and integration work before anything ships to customer floors. This is the company's manufacturing footprint going into the demo and Phase 1 pilots.

**Jade Molds** (Pat's company) — working production environment where AI-trained automation is validated against real manufacturing conditions before customer deployment. Functions as a captive test bed.

**China sourcing** — hardware components and assemblies sourced through Pat's vetted China supplier network for meaningful cost advantage vs. US-only competitors. Hardware-agnostic positioning means suppliers can swap without changing the value proposition (supply-chain-risk mitigation).

## 63. PHASED GO-TO-MARKET — Phase 1 + Phase 2 channels

Deliberate sequencing: validate the platform and generate revenue in technically simpler applications first; expand to harder ones using cash flow and named domain experts.

**Phase 1 (Now — fast-to-market):** Machine tending (loading/unloading CNC, presses, similar) · Palletizing (Programming Wizard primary use case) · Pick & place (general part transfer). Lowest integration risk; nearest to current product capability.

**Phase 2 (Next — capital-intensive / future):** Welding (SME identified) · Inspection (SME identified) · Surface finishing (force/torque control) · Random bin picking (robust 3D perception + grasp planning). Phase 2 is gated on Phase 1 traction and additional capital; SMEs for welding and inspection are already identified though not yet named publicly in the deck (pending decision).

## 64. SOFTWARE PILLARS — four capabilities (consolidates §4, §11, §54 references)

(1) **Program by Demonstration** — operator records video + narrates task → analyzed via API → draft robot program generated → operator reviews/edits → system learns from edits over time. Currently in debugging phase. API-first for quality; learning store accumulates NeuRobots's own proprietary dataset for eventual local-model replacement (see v19 §4 for the architecture decision). (2) **Programming Wizard** — guided no-code step-by-step flow for palletizing, pick & place; asks operator simple questions, teaches parts as needed, builds program automatically. In active development. (3) **Part Recognition** — camera-taught system distinguishes pickable vs. non-pickable orientations; controller retains taught orientations. In active development. (4) **3D + TCP Control** — 3D viewer with draggable tool center point for position-setting and motion-path preview before runtime. Integration in progress; current blocker is S10/S10-140 joint articulation in the viewer (see v19 §51 for the DH-accurate URDF path).

## 65. THE ASK + USE OF FUNDS — $1M for 10%

**Round:** $1M for 10% equity. ~$9M pre-money / $10M post-money. Pre-seed/seed. Priced round OR SAFE with $10M valuation cap. Top-of-market anchor based on hot AI/robotics conditions and Standard Bots' $1B comparable. Negotiating floor: $6-7M pre-money (~14-15% dilution) before walking in.

| Hardware & robot platforms | 35% | Robots, grippers, vision, bases |

**Primary:** "Robots that learn by watching." (title) · "Let's teach the machines." (closing). **Supporting punchlines used in deck:** "Video in. Working program out." · "Earn the right to the hard problems." · "We're not betting that AI will work in robotics. We're shipping it." · "They have the capital. We have the AI." · "Operators, not theorists." · "From demo to deployment." **Avoid in pitch:** generic "AI-native" claims (Standard Bots owns that air; differentiate by showing AI work, not claiming the label); humanoid robot framing (different market); over-promising on Phase 2 before Phase 1 traction is real.

## 69. PROCESS LESSONS — investor-materials work (extends §56/§41/§27/§13)

26. **Verify product positioning against the source-of-truth strategy doc before producing materials.** Multiple turns of deck work were built on a "AI-driven no-code programming platform" framing before the user confirmed the intended positioning is actually robot maker + AI platform (Standard Bots competitor) — a meaningful pivot from `document_pdf.pdf`'s "AI-native automation integrator" framing. Cost: rework of competitive slide, business model, and ask framing. Lesson: when project files contain a positioning doc, surface the conflict EARLY (turn 1 of materials work) rather than building forward on assumption.

27. **Team slides need real bios, not placeholders.** Initial team slide used `[Names/roles to be finalized]` and was visibly weakest part of the deck. Once real bios were provided (Josh's DBA + MFG Edge AI, Pat's Jade Molds, Teddy's Tesla + KIT), the slide became one of the strongest. Lesson for investor-materials work: get team backgrounds before generating, not after.

28. **Brand naming is iterative and expensive in tokens — get strategic direction first, then push availability.** Naming arc: Arcwell → Neuroforge → Neurobots/Neurobotix → finally NeuRobots Manufacturing. Each cycle required regenerating logo + wordmark + deck text + one-pager. Lesson: lock the strategic direction ("must have neuro," "must have bots," "must be available") before iterating on candidates. The wordplay stylization (capital R in NeuRobots) was the unlock — both the customer-facing wordplay and the visual brand mark fell out of one decision.

29. **Honest valuation framing protects credibility.** $1M-for-10% at $10M post-money is top-of-market for pre-revenue robotics — assertive based on Standard Bots' $1B comp and hot AI/robotics conditions. Materials reflect this with a stated negotiating floor ($6-7M pre-money) for in-room flexibility. Lesson: when picking valuations, name them explicitly as opening anchors, not commitments — and have the fallback in hand before delivery.

30. **Chinese investor materials need human review.** Simplified Chinese deck produced as a translation of the English deck (industrial robotics terminology generally landed: 视频示教编程 for "Program by Demonstration," 机床上下料 for "machine tending," 种子轮 for "seed round"). SAFE was kept in English with 协议 ("agreement") — reviewer may want to substitute 可转换债 (convertible note) depending on audience. Lesson: AI translation is a strong first draft, not a final draft — flag for native-speaker review explicitly.

31. **Editorial design philosophy beats template design.** First-pass deck used the same three-card layout on every slide (template-default-feeling). Rebuild used distinct layouts per slide (big-stat callouts, before/after splits, horizontal timeline, bar chart, hero typography on title/closing/ask). The rebuild felt like an investor deck rather than a startup template. Lesson: when materials feel generic, vary the layouts per slide before adding more visual polish — layout variety carries more weight than decoration.
